PR_C01_INTRO1::block-0:
This Brāhmaṇa portion is begun as an elaborate restatement of the meaning already enunciated in the mantras. The narrative of the questions of the seers and their answers, however, is for the praise of this knowledge (vidyā). Thus the Upaniṣad extols the knowledge by indicating that it is to be received only by those equipped with austerity, the year-long residence in the celibate life of a brahmacārin in the teacher's house, and the like; and that it is to be expounded only by teachers comparable to Pippalāda, who are as good as omniscient — and not by just anybody.

Moreover, since austerity, celibacy and the rest are pointed out as means, their performance becomes a duty incumbent upon the seeker —
PR_C01_V01: Sukeśā the son of Bharadvāja, Śaibya Satyakāma, Sauryāyaṇī of the Gārgya line, Kausalya the son of Aśvala, Bhārgava of the Vidarbha country, and Kabandhī Kātyāyana — these, devoted to Brahman, established in Brahman, seeking the supreme Brahman, came near to the venerable Pippalāda with sacrificial faggots in their hands, thinking, "He surely will tell us all that." || 1 ||
PR_C01_V01::block-0:
"Sukeśā" — that is his personal name; "Bhāradvāja" — the descendant of Bharadvāja. "Śaibya" — son of Śibi; "Satyakāma" is a personal name. "Sauryāyaṇī" — "Saurya" is the son of Sūrya, and "Sauryāyaṇi" is his descendant; the form "Sauryāyaṇī" with the long vowel is a Vedic licence. "Gārgya" — born in the lineage of Garga. "Kausalya" is a name; "Āśvalāyana" is the descendant of Aśvala. "Bhārgava" — descendant of the gotra of Bhṛgu; "Vaidarbhi" — born in the country of the Vidarbhas. "Kabandhī" is a name; "Kātyāyana" is the descendant of Katya — but the suffix is the "yuvan" affix (denoting a younger descendant) since his great-grandfather is still living.

These, "devoted to Brahman" (brahma-para), means that they had reached the lower Brahman (apara-brahman, that is, the conditioned Hiraṇyagarbha) as their highest goal so far; "established in Brahman" (brahma-niṣṭha) means that they were steadfast in the practices conducive to that. "Seeking the supreme Brahman" — that is, engaging in inquiry with the resolve, "What is that eternal reality which is to be known? Let us strive with all our heart to attain it!" — for the sake of attaining that, with the conviction "He alone will declare all this to us," they approached the teacher.

How did they approach? "With sacrificial faggots in their hands" — bearing bundles of firewood in their hands, they came near to the venerable, the worshipful, Pippalāda the teacher; "upasannāḥ" means they reverently drew close to him as disciples.
PR_C01_V02: To them that seer said: "Stay with me yet another year, with austerity, with brahmacarya and with faith. Then ask whatever questions you wish; if we know, we will tell you all." || 2 ||
PR_C01_V02::block-0:
To them, who had thus approached, that seer in fact spoke: "Yet again" — even though you yourselves are already practitioners of austerity from before, nevertheless here, with austerity (that is, with the restraint of the senses), and especially with brahmacarya, and with śraddhā (faith arising from theistic conviction, marked by reverent devotion) — "saṃvatsaraṃ saṃvatsyatha" — for the duration of one year, dwell well, intent on serving the teacher properly.

After that, "yathākāmaṃ" — without overstepping the desire of each one, in accordance with the subject in which each has the wish to know — ask the questions concerning those subjects. "If we shall come to know" — if we shall understand what you ask. The word "yadi" ("if") is used to display humility, not to indicate ignorance or doubt; for that the questions were in fact resolved is established by the very settlement of the questions later. "All that you have asked I shall declare to you" — such was his promise.
PR_C01_V03: Then Kabandhī Kātyāyana approached him and asked: "Bhagavan, from where indeed are these creatures born?" || 3 ||
PR_C01_V03::block-0: "Then" — after the lapse of the year — Kabandhī Kātyāyana, having drawn near, asked: "O venerable one, from what cause indeed are these creatures, beginning with brāhmaṇas, born — that is, brought into being?" The purport of this question is that the answer should declare what is the effect, what is the goal attained, of the conjoint practice of the lower knowledge (apara-vidyā, the meditations and the like) together with works (karma).
PR_C01_V04: To him he replied: "Verily, Prajāpati, desiring offspring, performed austerity. Having performed austerity, he produced a pair — Rayi (matter / food) and Prāṇa (the eater) — thinking, 'These two will produce manifold offspring for me.'" || 4 ||
PR_C01_V04::block-0:
To him, who had thus asked, he in fact spoke; for the dispelling of his doubt he says: "Desiring offspring" — wishing to project creatures from himself; "verily, Prajāpati," who, being the universal Self, formed at the beginning of the cycle by the conviction "I shall create the world" — that is, Hiraṇyagarbha, knowing as scripture declares and acting accordingly — became, at the dawn of the kalpa, the Lord of all creatures both moving and stationary about to be projected. He then "performed austerity" — that is, he reflected upon the knowledge formed in former births, the knowledge whose content is what scripture reveals; this reflection is here called tapas.

Then, having performed that austerity (i.e., having pondered the Vedic knowledge), he "produced a pair" — he brought forth a couple, the duality which serves as the very means of creation: namely, "Rayi" — that is Soma, food — and "Prāṇa" — that is Agni, the eater. Thinking, "These two — Agni and Soma, the eater and the food — will produce manifold offspring for me in many forms," — having thus reflected, he fashioned, in the order beginning with the cosmic egg, the sun and the moon.
PR_C01_V05: Verily the sun is Prāṇa, and the moon alone is Rayi. Rayi is indeed all this — both that which has form and that which is formless. Therefore form itself is Rayi. || 5 ||
PR_C01_V05::block-0:
There, the sun verily is Prāṇa — the eater, the fire. The moon alone is Rayi. Rayi alone is food, the soma. Thus this single Prajāpati is both the eater (the fire) and the food (the soma); they are but one couple — the difference between them is only that of principal and subordinate features.

How so? "Rayi indeed is food, this whole." What is "this"? "Whatever has form" (gross), "and whatever is formless" (subtle). Both the formed and the formless, since both stand in the role of food for the eater, are nothing but Rayi. Hence, distinct from the formless, that which is of the form of the formed — namely, mūrti — is precisely Rayi, food, since it is consumed by the formless eater.
PR_C01_V06: Now when the sun, rising, enters the eastern quarter, by that act he gathers the prāṇas of the east into his rays. When he illumines the south, the west, the north, the nadir, the zenith, the intermediate quarters — when he illumines all — by that very act he gathers all the prāṇas into his rays. || 6 ||
PR_C01_V06::block-0:
Likewise the formless one too — Prāṇa, the eater — is in fact everything, including all that is to be eaten. How so? "Now the sun, rising" — coming up, becoming visible to the eyes of beings — "when it enters the eastern quarter" by its own light, that is, pervades it. By that very pervasion of itself, all the prāṇas (i.e., all living beings) of the east, who are the food, it places in its rays — those rays which are forms of the sun's own self-illumination and which, being all-pervading, hold the creatures within their pervasion. "Saṃnidhatte" means he settles them within himself, i.e., makes them one with his own being.

In the same way, that which it enters — the south, the west, the north, the lower direction, the upper direction — and the "intermediate quarters" (the corners and sub-directions), and whatever else there is — "all" — "it illumines." By that pervasion of its own light it gathers "all the prāṇas," the living beings established in every direction, into its rays.
PR_C01_V07: He, this Vaiśvānara, of universal form, the Prāṇa, the fire, rises. This very thing has been declared by the Ṛk-mantra. || 7 ||
PR_C01_V07::block-0: He, this eater, the Prāṇa, is "Vaiśvānara" — the Self of all; "of universal form," since he is the very Self of all things; he is both the Prāṇa and the fire, this same eater. He "rises" — ascends — every day, making all the directions his own. This same fact, already enunciated, is also declared by the Ṛk-mantra (which follows).
PR_C01_V08: Of all forms, tawny with rays, possessed of all-knowing splendour, the supreme refuge, the one light that burns — the thousand-rayed, abiding in a hundred ways, the prāṇa of all creatures, this Sun rises. (8)
PR_C01_V08::block-0:
Viśvarūpam — of every form, the very form of all. Hariṇam — possessed of rays (raśmivat), since hari signifies the rays. Jātavedasam — in whom prajñāna, knowledge, has arisen and become manifest. Parāyaṇam — the resort of all prāṇas, the supreme refuge into which they retire. Jyotiḥ — the very eye of all living beings, the light by which seeing is possible. Ekam — one without a second (advitīyam) in this its cosmic role. Tapantam — performing the act of heating, illumining and ripening the worlds. Such is the Self, the Sun, that the knowers of Brahman (brahmavidaḥ) have known as none other than their own Self.

If it be asked, "Who is this whom they have so known?" — the mantra answers: sahasraraśmiḥ, of thousand and innumerable rays; śatadhā vartamānaḥ, abiding in a hundred ways, that is, dividing himself in many ways according to the diversity of creatures (prāṇi-bhedena); prāṇaḥ prajānām, the very prāṇa of all beings; eṣa sūryaḥ udayati, this Sun arises. Thus the gross sun seen daily and the inner Self of all beings are, for the knower, one and the same — and this is the upāsanā here taught.
PR_C01_V09: The year, verily, is Prajāpati; of him there are two paths — the southern and the northern. Those who worship saying, "What has been done by way of sacrifice (iṣṭa) and works of public utility (pūrta) is enough," — they win only the lunar world; they alone return again. Therefore these ṛṣis who desire offspring take the southern path. This, indeed, is rayi (food/matter), the path of the fathers. (9)
PR_C01_V09::block-0:
Now (it might be objected): The moon, embodied as food and form (mūrti), and the sun, the eater, formless prāṇa — these two together form one couple (mithuna); how can a single couple alone produce all these manifold creatures? To this the text replies — that very couple, viewed under the form of time, is the year, Prajāpati: "saṃvatsaro vai prajāpatiḥ." For the year is constituted (nirvartya) by them; the totality of the lunar tithis and the solar days and nights, made by sun and moon, is just the year. Being non-different (ananyatva) from these two, the year itself is of the very nature of the rayi-prāṇa couple.

How does Prajāpati, as the year, produce offspring? "Of him, the year, the Prajāpati, there are two paths (ayane), the southern (dakṣiṇa) and the northern (uttara)." The two ayanas of six months each are well known: by them the sun travels, southward and northward, ordaining the worlds for the merely ritualistic and for those whose action is joined with knowledge respectively.

In what way? "Tat" — there, in those, namely among brāhmaṇas and the rest, those ṛṣis who worship that. The second "tat" qualifies the act of worship. Iṣṭa (sacrificial offerings such as Agnihotra) and pūrta (works of public utility — wells, gardens, almshouses) — "that alone, as something done (kṛtam), they worship; not the not-done, the eternal (akṛtam, nityam)." These attain the lunar world (cāndramasam loka), the world born of the moon, the rayi portion of the mithuna-Prajāpati, of the nature of food (annabhūta) — for the lunar world too is itself something made (kṛta-rūpatva). Therefore, on the exhaustion of that made-merit, they return again, and "enter a still lower world," as has been declared elsewhere.

Since, then, by iṣṭa and pūrta these ṛṣis — householders desirous of offspring, beholders of svarga — accomplish only the food-bodied Prajāpati, the moon, as the fruit of their works, therefore their own self-made path, marked by the dakṣiṇāyana, leads them to the moon. "This indeed is rayi, food; that which is the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa)" — namely, the moon as designated by the pitṛyāṇa.
PR_C01_V10: But by the northern (path) — through tapas, brahmacarya, śraddhā, and vidyā — having sought out the Self, they win the Sun. This, verily, is the abode of the prāṇas; this is immortal, fearless; this is the supreme goal; from this they return no more. This (return) is, indeed, the obstruction (for the others). On this there is this verse. (10)
PR_C01_V10::block-0:
Atha, on the other hand: "by the uttara (path)," by the northern course, they win the sun, that aspect of Prajāpati which is prāṇa, the eater. By what means? "By tapas" — the conquest of the senses (indriya-jaya); especially "by brahmacarya," "by śraddhā," "and by vidyā" — knowledge having Prajāpati's Self for its object. Having sought out the Self — the prāṇa, the sun who is the inmost of all that moves and stands still — and having known, "I am He (aham asmi)," they win the sun, attain unto Him completely (abhi-prāpnuvanti).

"This, verily, is the āyatana" — the common resort, the support, of all the prāṇas. "This is amṛtam" — imperishable; "abhayam" — and for that very reason fearless, not subject to the fear of waxing and waning that besets the moon. "This is parāyaṇam" — the supreme goal, both for the men of vidyā and for those whose action is joined with knowledge. "From this they return no more," as do the merely ritualistic. "This" — that very return — "is the obstruction (nirodha)" of the unwise: for the unwise are obstructed by the sun himself; they do not reach the year, the sun, the Self, the prāṇa. He, the year, the very Self of time (kālātmā), is the obstructor of the ignorant. Tat — on that, on this very theme — eṣa ślokaḥ, this verse, this mantra, follows.
PR_C01_V11: They speak of the Father with five feet, of twelve forms, dwelling in the higher half of heaven, full of waters; while others again say He, the all-seeing, is fixed in the seven-wheeled, six-spoked (chariot of time). (11)
PR_C01_V11::block-0:
Pañcapādam — "five-footed": for this sun, of the nature of the year, has the five seasons (ṛtu) as his feet; by them, as by feet, he goes round and round. Here hemanta and śiśira are taken together as one, to make the count five. Pitaram — Father, because he is the begetter of all (sarvasya janayitṛtvāt). Dvādaśākṛtim — having twelve forms; the twelve months are his limbs (avayava), his "shaping," or that by which he is given limbs — therefore twelve-formed. Divaḥ pare ardhe — in the higher half above the heavenly region, that is, in the third heaven; pravṛtti-cakra of time abides there. Purīṣiṇam — possessed of purīṣa, that is, of waters: thus the knowers of time speak of him.

Now, again, others — other knowers of time — speak of that very same one as vicakṣaṇam, the discerning, the skilful, the all-knowing; arpitam, fixed like spokes in the nave of a chariot, in the saptacakra, in the seven-horsed wheel that is the all-pervading course of time, and in the ṣaḍara, that which has the six seasons as spokes. Whether one calls Him five-footed and twelve-formed, or seven-wheeled and six-spoked — in every way the year, the Self of time, Prajāpati marked by sun and moon, is the cause of the world.
PR_C01_V12: The month, verily, is Prajāpati: of him, the dark fortnight is rayi, the bright is prāṇa. Therefore these ṛṣis perform the sacrifice in the bright (fortnight); the others — in the other. (12)
PR_C01_V12::block-0:
He in whom this whole world is woven (protam) — that very Prajāpati, called the year, is fully comprehended in his own limb, the month: "māso vai prajāpatiḥ," the month, of the same character as already described, is itself the mithuna-Prajāpati. Of this month-Prajāpati, one part — the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa-pakṣa) alone — is rayi, food, the moon; the other part is śukla, the bright fortnight, prāṇa, the sun, the eater, fire.

Since these ṛṣis behold the bright fortnight, of the nature of prāṇa, as everything — they are prāṇa-darśins — therefore, even when they perform iṣṭa, the sacrifice, in the dark fortnight, they perform it as if in the bright fortnight alone; for they do not see a kṛṣṇa-pakṣa apart from prāṇa. Others, however, do not see prāṇa at all; they see only the kṛṣṇa-Self, of the nature of non-perception (adarśana-lakṣaṇa). Hence "itare itarasmin" — these others perform the sacrifice in the dark fortnight only, even when, externally, they perform it in the bright.
PR_C01_V13: Day-and-night, verily, is Prajāpati: of him, day alone is prāṇa, night alone is rayi. They do indeed slay prāṇa who unite with the woman in love by day; the union by night is itself brahmacarya. (13)
PR_C01_V13::block-0:
That month-Self Prajāpati too is fully comprehended in his own limb, day-and-night (ahorātra). "Ahorātro vai prajāpatiḥ" — as before. Of him too, day alone is prāṇa, the eater, the fire; night alone is rayi — exactly as before. Prāṇam — that is, prāṇa, having day for its Self — "these slay (praskandanti)," drive out, dry up, sever it from their own self and cast it away. Who? "Those who, by day, unite with their wife as the cause of pleasure (rati)" — that is, the deluded who indulge in maithuna by day. Since this is so, it should not be done — this is an incidental prohibition (prāsaṅgika-pratiṣedha).

"That which is union by night, in the fertile season, is brahmacarya itself" — being praiseworthy. Going to one's wife at night in season is therefore enjoined — this too is a prāsaṅgika-vidhi. The principal theme is now resumed: the same Prajāpati, of the nature of day-and-night, having now established himself as food in the form of rice, barley and the rest.
PR_C01_V14: Food, verily, is Prajāpati. From it, indeed, comes the seed; from that these creatures are born. (14)
PR_C01_V14::block-0: Having thus undergone successive transformation (krameṇa pariṇamya): "that food (annam) verily is Prajāpati." How? Tataḥ — from that food — the retas, the seed, the cause of progeny, arises in man (nṛ-bīja); and from that seed, when poured into the woman, these creatures of the form of men and the rest are born. This is the very answer to what was asked at the outset, "From what indeed are creatures born?" Thus, by the orderly succession beginning with the sun-moon couple and ending with day-and-night, by way of food and seed, these creatures are born — so it has been determined.
PR_C01_V15: Now, those who keep this Prajāpati-vow beget the (right) couple. To them alone belongs that Brahma-loka in whom tapas, brahmacarya, and truth are firmly established. (15)
PR_C01_V15::block-0: Tat — under these circumstances — those who are householders. Ha vai are particles indicating well-known recollection. They observe (caranti) the prajāpati-vrata, that is, going to one's wife in the fertile season — this is Prajāpati's own vow. To them, this is the seen fruit (dṛṣṭa-phala). What? They beget a mithuna — a son and a daughter. The unseen fruit (adṛṣṭa-phala) of those who perform iṣṭa, pūrta and dāna is this very lunar Brahma-loka, of the nature of the pitṛyāṇa, belonging only to those in whom tapas — namely the snātaka-vrata and the rest — and brahmacarya — namely the non-practice of maithuna outside the fertile season — and satya — the avoidance of falsehood — are unswervingly (avyabhicārataḥ) established (pratiṣṭhita), abiding always.
PR_C01_V16: Theirs is that stainless world of Brahman, in whom there is no crookedness, no falsehood, and no māyā. (16)
PR_C01_V16::block-0:
But the other Brahman-world, indicated by the sun and reached by the northern path (uttarāyaṇa), which is of the nature of the cosmic prāṇa-Self, is virajaḥ — pure and free from the dust of birth, growth and decay, unlike the lunar Brahman-world which is sullied by waxing and waning. That world is theirs — but of whom? This is now stated. Just as among householders, owing to their being engaged in many mutually conflicting transactions and aims, jihma — crookedness, the bent and twisted disposition — is unavoidable, so it is not present in those of whom this is said. And just as among householders falsehood (anṛta) is unavoidable on account of play and like occasions, so too it is absent in those. Likewise māyā, which exists among householders, is not present in them.

Māyā is that by which one displays oneself outwardly in one form and yet performs an action of an entirely different character — it is of the nature of false conduct. These defects, beginning with māyā, do not exist in those who are alone — the celibate students (brahmacārin), the forest-dwellers (vānaprastha), and the wandering mendicants (bhikṣu) — because the occasions for them are absent. In conformity with their respective means, theirs is this stainless world of Brahman: such is the goal of those whose works are joined with knowledge. The Brahman-world spoken of earlier, marked by the moon, belongs to those engaged in works alone.
PR_C02_V01: Then Bhārgava of Vidarbha asked him: "Sir, how many deities sustain the creature, which of them illumine this, and who again is the foremost among them?" (1)
PR_C02_V01::block-0: It has been said that Prāṇa is the eater and Prajāpati. The fact that he is Prajāpati and the eater must be ascertained as residing within this very body — and so this question is now begun. Then, immediately afterwards, indeed Bhārgava of Vidarbha asked him: "O revered one, how many deities (devāḥ) sustain prajā — that is, this body — viśeṣeṇa dhārayanti, hold it firmly together? Among the senses of knowledge and the senses of action, distributed thus, which of them illumine this — that is, manifest their own greatness? And who again is the foremost (variṣṭha), the chief, among these instruments of body and senses?"
PR_C02_V02: To him he then said: "Verily this deity is space, and air, fire, water, earth, speech, mind, eye, and ear. They, manifesting themselves, declare: 'It is we who, propping up this body, sustain it.'" (2)
PR_C02_V02::block-0:
To him who had thus questioned, he replied: ākāśaḥ ha vai eṣaḥ devaḥ — these very beings, namely space, air, fire, water and earth — are the five great elements that build up the body; and speech, mind, eye, ear and the rest are the senses of action and the senses of knowledge. These deities, of the nature of effects (the elements) and of instruments (the senses), manifest the greatness of the self that is to be revealed (prakāśya), and so abhivadanti — speak forth, vying with one another for the supremacy of the "I."

How do they speak? "We, propping up this 'reed' (bāṇa) — that is, this aggregate of body and senses — like pillars supporting a palace, holding it without slackening, sustain it firmly and visibly." The intent of each one severally is: "It is by me alone, single-handed, that this aggregate is upheld."
PR_C02_V03: To them the foremost, Prāṇa, said: "Do not fall into delusion. It is I alone who, dividing myself fivefold, prop up this body and sustain it." But they remained unbelieving. (3)
PR_C02_V03::block-0: To them, who had thus become full of self-conceit, the foremost — the chief — Prāṇa spoke: "Do not fall into such mohaḥ — delusion; do not, out of want of discrimination, take this prideful stance. For it is I alone who, propping up this body, sustain it: dividing myself fivefold, making the divisions of my own functions as prāṇa, apāna and the rest, I uphold this body." When he had spoken thus, they became aśraddadhānāḥ — without faith, without conviction — thinking, "How can this be so?"
PR_C02_V04: Out of indignation he made as if to depart upwards. As he departed, all the rest also rose to depart; and as he settled back, all settled back. Just as bees, when their king bee rises to depart, all rise; and as he settles, all settle — even so did speech, mind, eye, ear and the rest, pleased, praise Prāṇa. (4)
PR_C02_V04::block-0:
And that Prāṇa, observing their want of faith, out of self-respect made as if to depart upwards — as though, out of indignation, ignoring them; he behaved as one rising to leave the body. To make plain by example what happened when he so rose, the text now describes it: when he had risen to depart, then immediately all the rest — the senses, eye and so on — rose up after him, departing too. And when that Prāṇa settled back — became silent and did not depart — they all settled back, abiding silent and steady.

Just as in the world, when bees (madhukarāḥ) — that is, the bees in a hive — see their own king bee rising to depart, they all rise after him; and when he settles, they all settle and remain. As is this illustration, even so did speech, mind, eye, ear and the rest, abandoning their lack of faith, having recognised the greatness of Prāṇa, and being pleased, praise Prāṇa — they extolled him with hymns of praise.
PR_C02_V05: He it is that, as fire, burns; he is the sun; he is the rain-cloud, Maghavān (Indra); he is the wind; he is the earth, and matter (rayi); he is the deity; he is the existent and the non-existent, and that which is immortal. (5)
PR_C02_V05::block-0: How so? This Prāṇa, being fire, burns and blazes. So too, being the sun, he shines. So too, being the rain-cloud, he rains. Moreover, being Maghavān — Indra — he protects creatures and seeks to slay the asuras and rākṣasas. Furthermore, this very Prāṇa is the wind in its varied forms — āvaha, pravaha and the rest. And again, he is the earth and rayi (matter, food); he is the deity; he is the sat — the formed, gross — and the asat — the unformed, subtle — of the entire universe; and he is what is amṛta, the immortal, the cause that sustains the gods themselves.
PR_C02_V06: As spokes in the hub of a wheel, so is everything fixed in Prāṇa — the Ṛk verses, Yajus, Sāmans, the sacrifice, the kṣatriya power and the brahminhood. (6)
PR_C02_V06::block-0: What need to say more? As spokes are fixed in the hub of a wheel, so is everything — beginning with śraddhā and ending with nāma — during the period of subsistence, fixed in Prāṇa alone. So too the threefold mantras — the Ṛks, Yajuses and Sāmans — and the sacrifice that is to be accomplished by them; the kṣatra, which is the protector of all; and brahma, the brāhmaṇa class which is qualified as the agent of sacrifice and like rites — all this is this Prāṇa alone.
PR_C02_V07: As Prajāpati you move within the womb; you yourself are born again. To you, O Prāṇa, do these creatures bring offerings — to you who abide in all bodies along with the senses. (7)
PR_C02_V07::block-0: Moreover, even he who is Prajāpati is none other than you yourself: you move within the womb, and, becoming the very likeness of the father and the mother, you are born again (pratijāyase). Since you are Prajāpati, your fatherhood and motherhood of all creatures are established from the beginning. The meaning is: there is one Prāṇa, hidden under the forms of all bodies and embodied beings — he alone is the Self of all. To you — for your sake — these creatures, men and the rest, O Prāṇa, bring offerings (balim haranti) through the doors of the eye and the other senses. Since you, together with the prāṇas — that is, the eye and the rest — abide in all bodies, it is fitting that they bring offerings to you. You alone are the enjoyer; everything else is your food.
PR_C02_V08: Of the gods you are the foremost conveyer (of oblations); of the manes you are the first svadhā-offering. You are the true conduct of the seers, and of the Atharvans and Aṅgirases.
PR_C02_V08::block-0:
Furthermore, of the gods — Indra and the rest — you are vahnitamaḥ, that is, the foremost in conveying the oblations to them. And of the manes — at the nāndīmukha śrāddha, the svadhā, that is, the food which is offered to the manes, becomes the first when compared with what is offered to the gods. The meaning is that you alone are also the conveyer of that svadhā to the manes.

Furthermore, of the seers, namely the prāṇas such as the eye and the others, of the Atharvans who are also the Aṅgirases — for there is the śruti, ‘Their prāṇa indeed is Atharvan’ — the conduct, that is, the activity, the truth, the unfailing functioning characterised by the support of the body and so forth, you alone are.
PR_C02_V09: O Prāṇa, you are Indra; by your valour you are Rudra (the destroyer); you are also the all-around protector. You move in the mid-region; you are the sun, the lord of all luminaries.
PR_C02_V09::block-0:
Furthermore, O Prāṇa, you are Indra, the supreme Lord; by your valour, that is, by your power, you are Rudra, withdrawing the world (at the time of dissolution). And in the time of preservation you are pari, that is, on every side, the protector, the sustainer; you yourself, in your gentle form, are the all-around protector of the world.

You move ceaselessly in the mid-region by way of rising and setting (as the sun). You alone are the sun, and the lord of all luminaries.
PR_C02_V10: When you, O Prāṇa, pour down rain, then these creatures of yours stand forth in the form of bliss, (thinking) ‘there shall be food at our pleasure.’
PR_C02_V10::block-0:
When, having become Parjanya (the rain-cloud), you pour down rain, then, having obtained food, these creatures live and carry on the activities of life — that is the meaning. Or else, O Prāṇa, these creatures of yours, who are of your own nature, who are nourished by the food (which is) you, by the very sight of your raining stand forth as it were in the form of bliss, having attained happiness.

The purport is this: ‘food shall come into being for our desire, that is, in accordance with our wish.’
PR_C02_V11: O Prāṇa, you are the unconsecrated (vrātya), the one Ṛṣi, the eater (of oblations), the true lord of all that exists. We are the givers of the food (offered to you); you, O Mātariśvan, are our father.
PR_C02_V11::block-0:
Furthermore, since you are the firstborn and there exists no one else to consecrate you, you are the unconsecrated (vrātya); the meaning is that you are pure by your very nature.

O Prāṇa, you are the One Seer (Ekarṣi), being the fire well known among the Atharvans by the name Ekarṣi, the eater of all oblations. You yourself are the lord of all (vishva), of all that exists; or sat-pati means the good lord. We, on the other hand, are the givers of the food, that is, of the oblation eaten by you, the firstborn.

O Mātariśvan, you are our father; or, you are the father of Mātariśvan, that is, of Vāyu (the wind). And from this, your fatherhood with respect to the entire world stands established.
PR_C02_V12: That body of yours which is established in speech, which is in the ear, which is in the eye, and which is spread through the mind — make it auspicious; do not depart.
PR_C02_V12::block-0:
What more is to be said? That body of yours, which is established in speech as the speaker carrying on the activity of speaking, and which (is established) in the ear and in the eye, and which is spread through the mind by the operation of resolve and the rest — that body of yours, make it auspicious, that is, peaceful.

Do not depart; the meaning is, ‘do not, by departing, render it inauspicious.’
PR_C02_V13: Whatever exists here and whatever is established in the third heaven — all this is under the control of Prāṇa. As a mother (protects) her sons, so do you protect us; bestow upon us prosperity and wisdom.
PR_C02_V13::block-0:
What more is there to say? In this world, all this — whatever class of objects of enjoyment there be — is verily under the control of Prāṇa. And whatever is established in the third heaven (tridiva), characterised by the enjoyments of the gods and so on, of that too Prāṇa alone is the ruler and the protector.

Therefore, as a mother (protects) her sons, so protect us, sustain us. The brahmic and kshatriya glories, indeed, have you for their cause; bestow upon us those glories — śrī (prosperity) — and the wisdom (prajñā) by which we may abide.

Thus, in this manner, by the praise offered through the prāṇas of speech and the rest in the form of the universal Self, the greatness of Prāṇa has been declared, and it is firmly established that Prāṇa is verily Prajāpati himself.
PR_C03_V01: Then Kausalya, the son of Aśvala, asked him: ‘Sir, whence is this Prāṇa born? How does it come into this body? Or, having distributed itself, how does it stand firm? By what does it depart? How does it sustain the external (world) and how the inner (self)?’
PR_C03_V01::block-0:
‘Then, indeed, Kausalya, the son of Aśvala, asked him.’ When the truth (of Prāṇa) had thus been ascertained through (the praise by) the prāṇas, and his greatness had been comprehended, still — because he is composite (saṁhata) — there might be in him the character of a product (kārya); therefore I ask.

O Bhagavan, kutaḥ — from what cause — is this Prāṇa, ascertained as has been said, born? And being born, how — by what particular function — does it come into this body? The meaning is: what is the cause of his taking on a body?

And having entered the body, having distributed himself, ātmānaṁ vā pravibhajya — having made the division — how, that is, in what manner, does he stand firm, get established? And by what particular function does he depart out of this body? How does he sustain the external — that is, the adhibhūta and the adhidaivata? And how the adhyātma — the word ‘sustains’ being supplied here too?
PR_C03_V02: To him he replied: ‘You ask transcending questions; you are most steeped in Brahman; therefore I shall declare it to you.’
PR_C03_V02::block-0:
Thus questioned, ‘to him the teacher replied.’ Prāṇa himself, being hard to know, deserves only difficult questions; and yet you ask about his birth and the rest. Therefore you are asking ‘ati-praśnān’ — questions that go beyond (the ordinary).

‘Brahmiṣṭho ’si’ — you are eminently a knower of Brahman; therefore I am pleased; and so, ‘to you I shall declare’ — listen to what has been asked.
PR_C03_V03: From the Ātman this prāṇa is born. As is this shadow on a person, so is it (prāṇa) extended upon this (Self); through what is wrought by the mind it comes into this body.
PR_C03_V03::block-0:
From the Ātman, that is, from the supreme Puruṣa who is the imperishable, the Real (akṣara, satya), this aforementioned prāṇa is born. As to how, an illustration is given. Just as in the world this shadow, dependent upon a person possessing the marks of head, hands and the like as its nimitta (occasioning cause), is produced as a contingent (naimittika) effect, in the very same way, in this Brahman, this entity called prāṇa, which stands in the place of the shadow and is of the form of the unreal (anṛta), is extended upon, that is, deposited in, the true Puruṣa.

As the shadow exists in the body, so does prāṇa come here through what is wrought by the mind, that is, through karma accomplished by the mind's resolves, desires and the like. Indeed, it will be said further on, "by merit, the meritorious," and so on. From another scriptural passage too, "That very self, attached, goes along with its karma" (Br. Up. 4.4.6). Thus it comes, that is, arrives, into this body.
PR_C03_V04: Just as a sovereign emperor commissions his appointed officials, saying "Govern these villages, govern those villages," even so this prāṇa appoints the other prāṇas separately, each in its own place.
PR_C03_V04::block-0: Just as in the world, in the manner described, the king, the sovereign emperor, commissions those who are appointed over villages and the like. How? Saying, "Govern these villages, govern those villages." Even so, exactly as in this illustration, this chief prāṇa stations and commissions the other prāṇas, namely the eye and the rest, which are differentiations of itself, separately, each according to its proper station.
PR_C03_V05: In the organs of excretion and generation is apāna; in the eyes and ears, together with the mouth and nostrils, prāṇa itself abides; in the middle is samāna. For this (samāna) distributes equally what is offered as food; and from it arise these seven flames.
PR_C03_V05::block-0:
Now the distribution. In pāyu and upastha (the anus and the generative organ), together called pāyūpastha, in that, apāna, which is a differentiation of the Self and which performs the carrying off of urine, faeces and the like, is stationed and abides. So too in the eye and ear, conjointly called cakṣuḥśrotra, and going forth through the mouth and nostrils, called mukhanāsika, prāṇa itself, occupying the place of the sovereign, is firmly established. In the middle, that is, in the navel between the stations of prāṇa and apāna, is samāna; it is called samāna because it carries equally (samaṁ nayati) what is eaten and drunk.

For since this samāna distributes equally the food, that is, what is eaten and drunk and offered as oblation into the fire of the Self, therefore from the fire in the belly, kindled by the fuel of food and drink and reaching the region of the heart, these flames, seven in number, go forth as radiances. The intent is that, through the prāṇas seated in the head, the illumination of objects such as form is effected by way of seeing, hearing and the rest.
PR_C03_V06: In the heart verily is this Self. Here are these one hundred and one nāḍīs; of each of them there are a hundred branches, and of each branch seventy-two thousand sub-branches; in these vyāna moves.
PR_C03_V06::block-0:
"In the heart" - in the cavity of the heart bounded by the lump of flesh shaped like a lotus-bud, this Self, that is, the liṅga-ātman conjoined with the (subtle) self, the jīva-ātman, is meant. Here, in this heart, there are these one hundred and one principal nāḍīs in number. Of each of these principal nāḍīs there are a hundred branches; and again of each there are seventy-two thousand, that is, seventy thousand and two thousand more, sub-branch nāḍīs - thus, of each of the hundred sub-branches of the principal nāḍīs, there are these thousands.

In these nāḍīs the wind called vyāna moves. It is vyāna because of pervading (vyāpana). Just as the rays from the sun, so does vyāna, having pervaded the entire body through the nāḍīs that go forth in all directions from the heart, abide. At the joints, shoulders and vital spots especially, and in the interval between the operations of prāṇa and apāna, it becomes possessed of heightened activity and is the doer of vigorous deeds.
PR_C03_V07: Then by one of them, going upward, udāna leads by merit to the world of merit, by demerit to the world of demerit, and by both to the world of men.
PR_C03_V07::block-0: Now, of those one hundred and one nāḍīs, that one which goes upward, called suṣumnā - by that single nāḍī, going upward, the wind udāna, whose operation extends from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, journeys forth and leads, that is, brings, the soul through merit, that is, through karma sanctioned by the śāstra, to the meritorious world characterised by the abode of the gods and the like. Through demerit, the opposite of that, it leads to the world of demerit characterised by hell, the wombs of beasts and so on. By both together, that is, by merit and demerit equally predominant, it leads to the world of men - this verb "leads" is to be understood throughout.
PR_C03_V08: The sun verily is the outer prāṇa; it rises, favouring this prāṇa of the eye. The deity in the earth, she sustains the apāna of the person; what is between (the heaven and earth) is the ākāśa, that is samāna; the (general) wind is vyāna.
PR_C03_V08::block-0:
The sun, indeed - the well-known one - is the outer prāṇa on the side of the deities; that very one rises, that is, comes up. For he, by his light, favours this internal cakṣuṣa-prāṇa, that is, the prāṇa abiding in the eye, by furnishing illumination to the eye in its apprehension of form - this is the meaning. So too, the well-known deity who presides over the earth - she, by drawing down and subduing the operation of apāna in the person, by drawing it downward, becomes one who favours it; for otherwise the body, by reason of its weight, would fall, or, in open space, would float upward.

That which is the ākāśa between, that is, in the middle of, heaven and earth - the wind that abides in that ākāśa is itself called ākāśa, just as one seated on a couch (is called the couch). That is samāna; it abides as one favouring samāna - this is the meaning - because of the common feature of being seated in the inner ākāśa as samāna is. And likewise the wind that is outside in general, by the common feature of pervasiveness, is vyāna; it abides as one favouring vyāna - this is the intent.
PR_C03_V09: Heat verily is udāna. Therefore, when the heat (in the body) has subsided, one is born again, with the senses merging into the mind.
PR_C03_V09::block-0:
What is the well-known general heat that exists outside - that, in the body, favours udāna, that is, the udāna wind, by its own light - this is the intent. Since udāna, being of the nature of heat and favoured by the outer heat, is the agent of departure (utkrānti), therefore, when a person in the world becomes "upaśāntatejas," that is, one whose natural heat has subsided, then one is to know him as one whose lifespan is exhausted and who is about to die.

He again attains another "bhava," that is, another body. How? Together with the senses merging into the mind, that is, with speech and the rest entering into the mind.
PR_C03_V10: With whatever thought he is endowed, with that he goes to (joins) the prāṇa; the prāṇa, joined with heat, together with the Self, leads him to the world resolved upon.
PR_C03_V10::block-0:
At the moment of death, with whatever thought (citta) one is endowed, by that very citta, that is, by that resolve, this jīva, together with the senses, comes to the prāṇa, that is, to the operation of the chief prāṇa. The meaning is that, at the time of death, with the operations of the senses dwindled, he abides solely by the operation of the chief prāṇa. For at that time the kinsmen say, "He is breathing, he is alive."

And that prāṇa, being joined with the udāna-operation as the heat, together with the Self, that is, with the master, the experiencer, - thus this prāṇa joined with the udāna and its operation, in accordance with the force of meritorious and demeritorious karma, leads, that is, conveys, that experiencer to the world resolved upon, that is, to the world that has been intended.
PR_C03_V11: He who, knowing thus, knows the prāṇa — his progeny is not cut off; he becomes immortal. On this there is the following verse.
PR_C03_V11::block-0:
Whoever, thus knowing — that is, knowing the prāṇa as qualified by the special features already enunciated, namely, its origin (utpatti) and the rest — his fruit, both in this world (aihika) and in the world beyond (āmuṣmika), is now declared. "Na ha asya" — assuredly of such a knower the progeny (prajā), characterised as sons, grandsons and the like, is not cut off, is not severed. And when the body falls, by reason of his attaining identity-of-abode with prāṇa (prāṇa-sāyujya) he becomes immortal (amṛtaḥ), of a nature in which dying does not occur.

In that very sense, summarising the matter concisely, this present verse, this mantra, follows.
PR_C03_V12: Origin, advent, station, and lordship — the fivefold (manifestation) — and likewise the inner (presence) of prāṇa: knowing (these), one attains the immortal — one attains the immortal. Thus.
PR_C03_V12::block-0:
Utpatti — the origin from the supreme Self (Paramātman); āyati — the advent, the coming-in by way of mind-conditioned operation into this body; sthāna — the station, the standing in the seats such as the anus, the genital, and so on; vibhutva — the lordship, the very sovereignty by which, like a paramount emperor (samrāj), the prāṇa institutes its modal differences in fivefold manner (pañcadhā). Externally, in the form of the sun and the rest; and adhyātmam — within the body, abiding under the form of the eye and the other (sense-deities) — having known the prāṇa thus, one attains the immortal.

"Vijñāyāmṛtam-aśnute" — this is repeated twice in order to mark the conclusion of the matter of the praśna (the third question).
PR_C04_V01: Then Sauryāyaṇī Gārgya questioned him: "Bhagavan, in this person, what (powers) sleep? What in him remain awake? Which is that deva that sees dreams? To whom belongs this happiness? In what, indeed, do all become firmly established?"
PR_C04_V01::block-0:
Then (atha) Sauryāyaṇī Gārgya questioned him. By the foregoing three questions all that is the field of the lower knowledge (apara-vidyā) — the entire saṁsāra, the domain of the manifested (vyākṛta), bearing the marks of means and end (sādhya-sādhana), and impermanent — has been set forth and concluded. Now therefore commences the latter triad of questions, by which is to be expounded that which is unlike means-and-end, that which is without prāṇa and beyond the range of mind, supersensory, no object, auspicious, peaceful, unmodified, imperishable (akṣara), real (satya), accessible only to the higher knowledge (para-vidyā), denoted by the term "Puruṣa," both within and without, unborn.

For it has been said in the second Muṇḍaka: "Just as from a well-kindled fire sparks fly forth in their thousands akin to itself, so, dear one, from that imperishable (akṣara) various beings are born; and there too they return." — Now (the question is): What are those various beings that, parted off from the akṣara, become divided as it were like sparks? And how, divided thus, do they return back into that very (akṣara)? And what is the characteristic mark of that akṣara? — Wishing to expound this, he now raises the questions.

"Bhagavan! In this puruṣa" — this person who has head and hands and so on — "what (organs) sleep" — that is, sink into slumber, withdraw from their own operations? "And what in him remain awake" — which carry on their own operation, that state which is wakefulness, the state of non-sleep? "Of the two — the body-and-organs (kārya-karaṇa) — which is that deva that sees dreams?" Now "dream" (svapna) is, for him who has withdrawn from waking-perception, that perceiving — internal to the body — which is like the perception of waking. Is it accomplished by the deva of the kārya-class (the body), or by some deva of the karaṇa-class (an organ)? — that is the import.

"And when the operations of waking and dream have ceased, that serene happiness (sukha), characterised by absence of strain, free from obstruction — to whom does this belong?" "At that time, having withdrawn from the activity of waking and dream, in what indeed do all" — well merged, become as one — "come to be sam-pratiṣṭhita" — established together? Like the rasa established in honey, like rivers and the rest entered into the ocean and incapable of being severally distinguished — even so they come to be conjoined, settled together. That is the meaning.

Objection (pūrvapakṣa): Just as a sickle and the like, when laid aside, abide each separately in its own place when withdrawn from its operation — even so it is fitting that the organs in their own selves stand each apart. Whence then arises in the questioner the apprehension that the organs of one in deep sleep go to some unitary state (ekī-bhāva)?

Reply (siddhānta): The apprehension is altogether reasonable. For the organs are aggregated together (saṁhata), they exist for the sake of an owner (svāmin), and they are dependent upon another (paratantra) in the field of waking. Therefore in sleep too, by their very dependence-upon-another, it is logical that the aggregated organs come to a coalescence in something. Hence this question conforms exactly to that apprehension. Here, then, that aggregate of body-and-organs (kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta) — in which it gets dissolved during deep-sleep and dissolution — wishing to know that very particular: "Who, then, can it be? In what indeed do they all come to be firmly established?"
PR_C04_V02: To him he, the teacher, said: "As, O Gārgya, the rays of the setting sun all become one in that disc of light, and they spread forth again when it rises again, even so, verily, all that becomes one in the supreme deva, the mind. Therefore at that time this person hears not, sees not, smells not, tastes not, touches not, speaks not, takes not, enjoys not, casts not forth, moves not — 'he sleeps,' so they say."
PR_C04_V02::block-0:
To him the teacher said: "Listen, O Gārgya, to that which thou hast asked. Just as the rays (marīcayaḥ), the beams of the sun (arkasya), of him who is going to setting (asta — his disappearance from view), all (sarvāḥ) — without remainder — become one (ekī-bhavanti) in this disc of light (tejo-maṇḍala), the mass-of-radiance: that is, they go to incapacity-of-distinction, to non-differentiation. And they, those very rays, of that very sun rising again and again (punaḥ punaḥ udayataḥ), spread forth (pracaranti), are scattered abroad. Such is this illustration.

Even so (evam ha vai), all that — the entire host of objects, organs, and the rest — becomes one in the supreme (pare), the eminent deva (deve), the luminous (dyotanavati): the mind (manasi). Since the devas like the eye, etc., are dependent on the mind (manas-tantratva), the supreme deva is the mind. In it, in dream-time, all becomes one (ekī-bhavati) — like the rays in the disc, it goes to non-differentiation. And of one wishing again to wake, like the rays from the disc, they go forth from the mind itself, get established for their own operations.

Since at the time of dream the ear and the rest — the organs that bring about the apprehension of sound and so on — have, as it were, become one (ekī-bhūtāni iva) in the mind, having withdrawn from the operation of the organs — "tena tarhi" — therefore at that time of sleep, this puruṣa, characterised as Devadatta or whoever, hears not, sees not, smells not, tastes not, touches not, speaks not, takes not, enjoys not, casts not forth, moves not — "he sleeps," so the people of the world say.
PR_C04_V03: The fires of prāṇa alone keep awake in this city. The Gārhapatya (fire), verily, is the apāna; the vyāna is the Anvāhāryapacana; since the Āhavanīya is led forth (praṇīyate) from the Gārhapatya, by reason of this leading-forth the prāṇa is the Āhavanīya.
PR_C04_V03::block-0:
When the organs such as the ear are as it were asleep, in this city — this nine-gated body — the prāṇa-fires, namely the prāṇas themselves, the five vāyus that are like fires, remain awake. He now states wherein lies their general likeness to fire.

"The Gārhapatya, verily, is the apāna." How so? — He explains. From the Gārhapatya fire, at the time of the agnihotra-rite, the other fire, the Āhavanīya, is led forth (praṇīyate); from this leading-forth — "that from which it is led forth" — the Gārhapatya is the praṇayana (the source-of-leading-out) of the fire. So too, of the sleeping man, by virtue of the apāna's operation, the prāṇa is, as it were, led forth (praṇīyate iva); it courses through mouth and nostrils — hence the prāṇa stands in the place of the Āhavanīya.

The vyāna, however, since it issues from the heart through the right (dakṣiṇa) channel-opening and is connected with the southern direction (dakṣiṇa-dik), corresponds to the Anvāhāryapacana — the southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni).
PR_C04_V04: Inasmuch as it leads the two oblations — out-breath and in-breath — equally, therefore it is the samāna. The mind, verily, is the yajamāna (sacrificer). The fruit of the sacrifice (iṣṭa-phala), assuredly, is the udāna; it leads this yajamāna day by day to Brahman.
PR_C04_V04::block-0:
And here, of the agnihotra, there is also a hotṛ. Inasmuch as (yat) the out-breath and in-breath (ucchvāsa-niḥśvāsau), like the two oblations of agnihotra (āhutī iva), constantly, by virtue of the very general fact of being two, those two āhutīs (etau āhutī) are led equally (samaṁ nayati), evenly, for the maintenance-of-the-body — the wind that, although it stands in the place of fire, is also the hotṛ, since it is the leader of the oblations — who is that? "saḥ samānaḥ" — he is the samāna.

Hence even the sleep of a knower (vidvān) is itself the offering of the agnihotra. Therefore the knower must not be thought of as one who has done away with action — that is the import. As is said in the Vājasaneyaka: "All beings everywhere, even when they sleep, perform agnihotra."

Now here, when the prāṇa-fires are awake, withdrawing into them the external organs and the objects, even as one would seek to attain heaven (the agnihotra-fruit), so wishing to attain Brahman, the mind (manaḥ) is verily the yajamāna who keeps awake. Since, like a yajamāna, the mind among the body-and-organs is principally engaged in transactional dealing, and since it sets out, as it were, towards Brahman as towards heaven, it is conceived as the yajamāna.

"Iṣṭa-phalam" — the very fruit of the sacrifice — is the udāna, the wind. For it is by means of the udāna that the attainment of the iṣṭa-phala (Brahman) takes place. How? — That udāna leads this very mind, denominated yajamāna, dislodging it even from the mode of dream-functioning, day by day (ahar ahaḥ) at the time of suṣupti, to Brahman, the akṣara — even as one is led to heaven. Therefore the udāna stands in the place of the fruit of the sacrifice.
PR_C04_V05: Here, in dream, this deva experiences greatness. Whatever has been seen he sees again as seen; whatever has been heard, he hears again as heard; what has been directly experienced through different places and quarters, he experiences again and again. The seen and the unseen, the heard and the unheard, the experienced and the unexperienced, the existent and the non-existent — he sees all; being all, he sees.
PR_C04_V05::block-0:
Thus, of a knower, from the time of the cessation of the ear and the rest until he rises from sleep, all that is, becomes nothing but the experiencing of the fruits of all sacrifices — not, as for the unwise, becoming a cause of evil. Thereby the knower's status is being extolled. For it is not only of the wise that the ear and the rest sleep, or only in whom the prāṇa-fires keep awake. Common alike to all living beings is the going of mind, in turn, to waking, to dream, and to deep-sleep. Hence what is here suitable is just the eulogy of knowership.

As to what was asked — "which is that deva that sees dreams?" — to that he replies. "Atra" — here — that is, when the ear and the rest have ceased, while the prāṇa and other vāyus remain awake for the protection of the body, in the interval prior to the attainment of suṣupti — "eṣa devaḥ" — this deva (the mind), having withdrawn the organs of ear and the rest into himself like the rays of the sun, in dream experiences greatness (mahimānam) — sovereignty, the going to a state of multiple selfhood, marked by the relation of subject and object.

Objection: For one experiencing greatness, the mind is the instrument of the experiencer; how then is it said that he experiences with svātantrya (independence)? It is the kṣetrajña (knower-of-the-field) alone who is svatantra (independent).

Reply: There is no fault here. The svātantrya of the kṣetrajña is brought about by the upādhi (limiting condition) of mind. The kṣetrajña does not, in the supreme reality, by himself either sleep or wake; both his waking and his dreaming are caused by the upādhi of mind. It has been said in the Vājasaneyaka: "Becoming a dreamer of pure intelligence (sa-dhīḥ svapnaḥ)," "He as it were thinks, he as it were quivers," and so on. Therefore in the experiencing of greatness through the mind, the assertion of svātantrya is itself proper.

Some contend: If one were associated with the mind-upādhi, then in dream-time the self-luminosity (svayam-jyotiṣṭva) of the kṣetrajña would be impeded. — That is not so. Theirs is a delusion born of non-comprehension of the import of the śruti. For all the talk of self-luminosity and so on — extending up to liberation (āmokṣāntaḥ) — itself falls within the field of avidyā, generated by the upādhis like mind, etc. As the śruti says: "Where there is, as it were, another, there one might see another" (Bṛ.U. 4.3.31), and "But where for him all has become his very Self, then by what should he see what?" (Bṛ.U. 4.5.15). Hence this misgiving belongs only to the dull-witted Brahman-knowers, not to those who know the One Self.

Objection: That being so, the qualification "Here this puruṣa is self-luminous" (Bṛ.U. 4.3.14) becomes purposeless.

Reply: This is too feeble an objection. By the (other) text "He lies in this ākāśa within the heart" (Bṛ.U. 2.1.17), where the inner-heart is made the limiting locus, all the more should self-luminosity be impeded.

If it be urged: "True; even so, in dream, by means of self-luminosity standing alone, half the burden has at least been lifted" — no, this is not so; for there too the śruti says "He lies in the purītat, in the channels." By the connection with the purītat and the channels, the intent that, in dream, by the puruṣa's self-luminosity, half the burden is lifted, is utterly vain.

Then how is "Here this puruṣa is self-luminous" (Bṛ.U. 4.3.14) to be taken? — If it be said: "That is from another śākhā and so to be disregarded," — no; for the unity of meaning is the desired conclusion. The one Ātman is the meaning that all the Vedānta-texts seek to make known, and which all seekers desire to know. Hence it is fitting to declare the establishment of the Ātman's self-luminosity in dream, since the śruti is the revealer of reality as it truly is.

Well then — listen to the meaning of the śruti, abandoning all conceit; for not even in a hundred years, by mere conceit, can the meaning of the śruti be known. (The bhāṣya as preserved here is truncated at this point.)
PR_C04_V06: When he becomes overpowered by tejas (luminous heat), then in this body this deva sees no dreams; then this happiness arises in this body.
PR_C04_V06::block-0:
He — the deva of the form of mind — at whatever time he becomes overpowered (abhibhūtaḥ) all around by the solar tejas (sūrya-related), called by the name pitta (bile), which abides in the channels (nāḍī-śaya), then his door-of-vāsanā becomes obstructed; at that time, together with the organs, the rays of the mind become withdrawn into the heart.

When mind, like fire in firewood, abides pervading the entire body in the form of undifferentiated cognition (a-viśeṣa-vijñāna-rūpeṇa), then he becomes one in deep sleep (suṣupta).

"Atra" — at this very time — "eṣa devaḥ" — this deva called mind — sees no dreams, the door of perception having been blocked by the tejas. "Atha" — and then — at this very time, in this body, this happiness (etat sukham) arises — that is to say, the cognition becomes obstructionless, undifferentiatedly pervading the body, and altogether serene (prasanna). That is the import.
PR_C04_V07: Just as, dear one, birds repair to their roosting-tree, so verily does all this come to rest in the supreme Self.
PR_C04_V07::block-0:
At this juncture — the time of deep sleep, and supremely so at the dissolution called liberation — the body and the organs (kāryakaraṇāni), which are bound together by avidyā, desire, and karma (avidyā-kāma-karma-nibandhanāni), become quiescent. When they are quiescent, the very nature of the Self (ātma-svarūpa), which had been made to appear otherwise through the upādhis, becomes non-dual, one, auspicious, peaceful (advayam ekaṁ śivaṁ śāntam). To exhibit precisely this state — by way of the merging of the modifications wrought by avidyā, namely earth and the rest, into their causes — Śaṅkara now provides an illustration.

The illustration runs thus: "yathā" — in the manner in which; "hi somya," O dear-faced one (priya-darśana); "vayāṁsi," the birds; for the sake of dwelling (vāsa-artham), to a tree, hence "vāso-vṛkṣam" (the dwelling-tree, samāsa-vigraha: vāsāya vṛkṣaḥ), they advance, that is, they go (sampratiṣṭhante = gacchanti). "Evam," just as in the illustration, "ha vai tat" — verily that, all that which is about to be enumerated, comes to rest in the supreme Self, the imperishable Akṣara (pare ātmani akṣare sampratiṣṭhate).
PR_C04_V08: Earth and the subtle essence of earth; water and the subtle essence of water; fire and the subtle essence of fire; air and the subtle essence of air; ākāśa and the subtle essence of ākāśa; the eye and what is to be seen; the ear and what is to be heard; the nose and what is to be smelled; taste and what is to be tasted; the skin and what is to be touched; speech and what is to be spoken; the hands and what is to be grasped; the genitals and what is to be enjoyed; the anus and what is to be excreted; the feet and what is to be travelled to; the mind and what is to be thought; the intellect and what is to be ascertained; the I-sense and what is to be claimed as "I"; the citta and what is to be cognised; the lustre and what is to be illumined; prāṇa and what is to be sustained.
PR_C04_V08::block-0:
What is that "all this" which comes to rest? "Pṛthivī ca" — the gross earth, possessed of five qualities (pañca-guṇā); and its cause, "pṛthivī-mātrā," the smell-tanmātrā (gandha-tanmātrā). Likewise water and the water-tanmātrā; fire and the fire-tanmātrā; air and the air-tanmātrā; ākāśa and the ākāśa-tanmātrā — meaning, both the gross and the subtle elements (sthūlāni ca sūkṣmāṇi ca bhūtāni).

Likewise the eye, the organ, and what is to be seen, namely form (rūpaṁ ca draṣṭavyam); the ear and what is to be heard; the nose and what is to be smelled; taste and what is to be tasted; the skin and what is to be touched; speech and what is to be spoken; the hands and what is to be grasped; the upastha and what is to be enjoyed; the anus and what is to be excreted; the feet and what is to be travelled to. Thus the cognitive senses (buddhi-indriyāṇi), the action senses (karma-indriyāṇi), and their respective objects have been declared.

"Manaḥ" — the mind already spoken of; "mantavyam," its object. "Buddhi" — that whose nature is determination (niścayātmikā); "boddhavyam," its object. "Ahaṅkāra" — the inner instrument characterised by the sense of "I" (abhimāna-lakṣaṇa-antaḥkaraṇa); "ahaṅkartavyam," its object. "Citta" — the inner instrument as endowed with awareness (cetanāvad antaḥkaraṇa); "cetayitavyam," its object.

"Tejas ca" — over and above the skin-organ, that skin which is distinguished by luminosity; through it the object made manifest, namely "vidyotayitavyam," what is to be illumined. "Prāṇa ca" — what they call the sūtra (the thread-self); by it "vidhārayitavyam," that which is to be sustained, that is, to be strung together (saṅgrathanīya). For the entire aggregate of body and organs is, by virtue of serving another (pārārthyena), bound together as a heap that is nothing but name and form (nāma-rūpa-ātmaka) — and just this much, no more.
PR_C04_V09: He, verily, is the seer, the toucher, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the cogniser, the doer — the knowing-self, the puruṣa. He comes to rest in the supreme imperishable Self.
PR_C04_V09::block-0:
Beyond these, that which is the very nature of the Self — that which has, like the sun reflected in water (jala-sūryaka), entered here through (apparent) enjoyership and agency (bhoktṛtva-kartṛtvena anupraviṣṭam) — "eṣa hi," this very one is the seer, the toucher, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the cogniser, the doer, the vijñāna-ātman.

Nirvacana of "vijñāna": that by which one knows is "vijñānam" — the buddhi and the like, taken as the karaṇa (instrument); but here "this one knows" — "vijānāti iti vijñānam" — taken as the kartṛ-kāraka, the agent. "Tad-ātmā" — having that as its very nature, that is, of the nature of the knower (vijñātṛ-svabhāva).

"Puruṣaḥ" — by reason of filling up (pūraṇa) the upādhi declared as the aggregate of body and organs, he is called puruṣa. And he, just like the reflected sun in water re-entering the sun when its supporting water is dried up (jalādy-ādhāra-śoṣe), comes to rest in the supreme imperishable Self (pare akṣare ātmani sampratiṣṭhate).
PR_C04_V10: He attains the supreme Imperishable itself — he who, O dear one, indeed knows that shadowless, bodiless, bloodless, pure Imperishable. Such a one becomes all-knowing, becomes all. On this very point there is this verse.
PR_C04_V10::block-0:
He now declares the fruit attained by the knower of that oneness: "param eva akṣaraṁ pratipadyate" — he attains the supreme Imperishable itself, characterised as is about to be stated. This is what is being said.

"Sa yo ha vai tat" — he who, freed from all cravings (sarva-eṣaṇā-vinirmuktaḥ), knows that — "acchāyam," devoid of darkness (tamo-varjitam); "aśarīram," devoid of every body that is an upādhi consisting of name and form (nāma-rūpa-sarva-upādhi-śarīra-varjitam); "alohitam," devoid of red and all such qualities (lohita-ādi-sarva-guṇa-varjitam); and since it is so, therefore "śubhram," pure (śuddham); since devoid of every distinguishing mark, "akṣaram," the Imperishable; the Real, designated puruṣa, prāṇa-less, beyond the range of the mind, auspicious, peaceful, with both outside and inside (sa-bāhya-abhyantaram), unborn (ajam) — he who knows this, he who has renounced everything (sarva-tyāgī), O somya — "sa sarvajñaḥ," he is all-knowing; nothing whatever remains unknown to him.

Formerly, through avidyā, he was not all-knowing; again, through vidyā, on the removal of avidyā, he becomes all (sarvaḥ bhavati). On this matter, this verse — a mantra summarising the meaning declared — comes next.
PR_C04_V11: In which the knowing-self together with all the deities, the prāṇas and the elements come to rest — that Imperishable he who knows, O dear one, becomes all-knowing and has entered into all.
PR_C04_V11::block-0:
"Vijñāna-ātmā" — the knowing-self; "saha devaiś ca," together with the deities, namely Agni and the rest; "prāṇāḥ," the eye and the other prāṇas; "bhūtāni," the elements earth and the rest; "sampratiṣṭhanti" — they enter, "praviśanti," "yatra," in which Imperishable.

That Imperishable — "yas tu vedayate," he who indeed knows it, "he somya," O dear-faced one — "sa sarvajñaḥ," he becomes all-knowing; "sarvam eva āviveśa" — he has entered into all, that is, he pervades all (āviśati), such is the sense.
PR_C05_V01: Then Śaibya Satyakāma asked him: "Bhagavan, he among men who, until the very moment of death, should meditate upon the syllable Om — which world, indeed, does he conquer thereby?"
PR_C05_V01::block-0:
"Atha ha enaṁ śaibyaḥ satyakāmaḥ papraccha." Now, at this point, with the intention of enjoining the upāsanā of Oṁkāra as the means to the attainment of both the para and the apara Brahman, the question is begun.

"Sa yaḥ kaścit ha vai bhagavan" — he, whoever, O Bhagavan; "manuṣyeṣu," amongst men; "tat," that — wonderful, as it were; "prāyaṇa-antam," up to the moment of departure, that is, lifelong (yāvaj-jīvam); "oṅkāram abhidhyāyīta," should meditate (cintayet) facing it directly (ābhimukhyena).

The meaning of "abhidhyāna" is this: with the senses withdrawn from external objects, with mind well-collected, with Brahman-intentness installed by devotion, a continuous unbroken stream of self-conviction (ātma-pratyaya-santāna-avicchedaḥ) directed upon Oṁkāra, made altogether free from cognitions of a different kind (bhinna-jātīya-pratyaya-akhilīkṛtaḥ), and resembling the flame of a lamp in a place free of wind (nivāta-stha-dīpa-śikhā-samaḥ).

Supported by the many yamas and niyamas — truth, brahmacarya, non-violence, renunciation of acquisition, samnyāsa, purity, contentment, freedom from deceit, and the rest — he, observing the vow lifelong: "katamaṁ vāva" — many indeed are the worlds that stand to be won by jñāna and karma; among them, by that meditation upon Oṁkāra, which world does he conquer?
PR_C05_V02: To him he answered: "O Satyakāma, this Oṁkāra is verily the supreme and the lower Brahman. Hence the wise, taking just this as the support, attains the one or the other."
PR_C05_V02::block-0:
To him who had thus questioned, Pippalāda said: "Etad vai satyakāma" — this, O Satyakāma. "Param ca aparaṁ ca brahma" — both the higher and the lower Brahman; the higher being the Real, Imperishable, called puruṣa; the lower being that called prāṇa, the first-born (prathama-ja); "yat," that — this is just Oṁkāra, of the very nature of Oṁkāra, since Oṁkāra is its symbol (pratīka).

For the supreme Brahman, being unfit to be designated by speech and the other indicators (śabda-ādi-upalakṣaṇa-anarham), being devoid of every distinguishing attribute (sarva-dharma-viśeṣa-varjitam), is, on account of being beyond the range of the senses, not capable of being grasped by the mind alone. But upon Oṁkāra — which stands like the images of Viṣṇu and the rest, and into which Brahman-intentness is installed by devotion — Brahman, it is understood from the authority of the śāstra, becomes graciously present to the meditators. So too with the supreme Brahman.

Hence both the higher and the lower Brahman are figuratively spoken of as "Oṁkāra" (upacaryate). Therefore one who knows in this manner, by just this means of attaining the Self, namely the abhidhyāna of Oṁkāra, "ekataram" — the one or the other, the higher or the lower — "anveti," attains, follows in the wake of Brahman; for Oṁkāra is verily the closest support (nediṣṭham ālambanam) of Brahman.
PR_C05_V03: If he should meditate upon it as one mātrā only, then, awakened by that very thing, he attains swiftly upon the earth. The Ṛk verses lead him to the world of men; there, endowed with austerity, brahmacarya and faith, he experiences greatness.
PR_C05_V03::block-0:
Even though one is not the knower of all the divisions of the mātrās of Oṁkāra, still, by the very efficacy of the meditation upon Oṁkāra, he attains a distinguished course; he does not fall into evil destiny because of the deficiency of partial knowledge — for, having taken refuge in Oṁkāra, he is not, like one fallen from both karma and jñāna, lost. Then what?

If he meditates only thus, knowing only the single-mātrā division (eka-mātrā-vibhāga-jñaḥ kevalaḥ), "ekamātram abhidhyāyīta" — should meditate ever upon the one mātrā — then, "sa tena eva," by that very meditation upon Oṁkāra qualified by the single mātrā, "saṁveditaḥ," awakened, fully informed (sambodhitaḥ), "tūrṇaṁ kṣipram eva," swiftly indeed, "jagatyāṁ pṛthivyām abhisampadyate," he attains upon the earth.

What does he attain? The world of men. For many are the births that occur upon the earth; among those, the Ṛks lead, that is, escort (upanigamayanti), that aspirant onto the world of men itself. The first single mātrā of Oṁkāra is, indeed, of the form of the Ṛg-veda. By that, he, in this human birth, being foremost among the twice-born (dvijāgryaḥ), endowed with tapas, brahmacarya and śraddhā, "mahimānam anubhavati" — experiences greatness, glory (vibhūtim); he does not become one of broken faith, given to wayward conduct (yathā-iṣṭa-ceṣṭaḥ). One fallen from yoga never at any time goes to evil destiny.
PR_C05_V04: Then if one attains [contemplation] by two mātrās, he becomes united with the manas; by the Yajus mantras he is led up to the inter-space, the world of Soma. Having experienced grandeur in the world of Soma, he returns again. (4)
PR_C05_V04::block-0:
“Now again,” — if one who knows the division of the two mātrās meditates on the Oṅkāra as qualified by the two mātrās, he attains, that is, with one-pointedness reaches identity in the manas — the manas which has the nature of dream, which is the proper object of meditation, which is constituted of the Yajus and presided over by Soma as its deity. Such a one, when he dies thus identified, is led up to the antarikṣa — that is, to the inter-space which is the support of the second mātrā, having the form of the second mātrā — and he is led up by the Yajus mantras themselves, which have the form of the second mātrā. The meaning is: those Yajus-mantras bring him to the world of Soma, the lunar realm, by way of birth there.

He, having experienced grandeur (vibhūti) there in the world of Soma, returns again towards the world of men. The two-mātrā meditation, being a mixed upāsana that does not transcend the realm of action, yields a fruit that is exhausted by enjoyment; therefore the return is inevitable. This is the path of pravṛtti, and it is here distinguished from the higher trajectory of the next mantra in order to expose, by contrast, the unsurpassed fruit of the three-mātrā contemplation that follows.
PR_C05_V05: But he who meditates on the supreme Puruṣa with this very syllable Om of three mātrās, becomes united in the radiance, the sun. Just as a snake is freed from its slough, even so verily is he freed from sin. He is led up by the Sāmans to the world of Brahman. From this dense aggregate of jīvas he beholds the Puruṣa higher than the highest, who lies in the city [of the body]. On this there are these two verses. (5)
PR_C05_V05::block-0:
“But he who meditates” on this Oṅkāra by means of three mātrās — that is, qualified by the knowledge that has the three mātrās as its sphere — “by this very syllable Om” meditates on the supreme Puruṣa, who is within the sun, taking the syllable as a symbol (pratīka). Why must the Puruṣa be taken as “symbol” and not as instrument here? Because by such meditation it is the role of ālambana (object of dependence) that is in question, and the Oṅkāra — being already the topic — has been declared by śruti to be both the higher and the lower Brahman without distinction. Otherwise, the second-case ending heard repeatedly with respect to the Oṅkāra would have to be set aside.

Granted, the third-case ending could be construed instrumentally — “by means of [the syllable] which has three mātrās”; but according to the maxim ‘one should sacrifice the single member for the sake of the family’ (tyajed ekaṃ kulasyārthe), it is more proper, in keeping with the topic, to construe ‘the three-mātrā [syllable] as the supreme Puruṣa’ in the second case. Such a one, while meditating, becomes united in the radiance, in the sun, which is of the form of the third mātrā. Even when he dies, he does not return as he did from the world of Soma earlier; rather, he becomes united in the sun forthwith.

“As a snake (pādodaraḥ — that which moves on its belly) is freed from its slough,” and being thus freed from its worn-out skin becomes new again — “even so verily,” taking this for the simile, “he is freed from sin,” that is, freed from the form of impurity which corresponds to the snake's slough. He is led up — upwards — by the Sāmans, of the form of the third mātrā, to the world of Brahman, namely the world of Hiraṇyagarbha, the Brahman called Satya.

That Hiraṇyagarbha is the inner Self of all transmigrating jīvas; for he is the antarātman of all beings in the form of the subtle body (liṅga). In him, as the liṅgātman, all jīvas stand aggregated. Therefore he is the “dense aggregate of jīvas” (jīvaghana). The wise one, who knows the three-mātrā Oṅkāra, beholds — that is, sees while meditating — from this jīvaghana, from Hiraṇyagarbha, the Puruṣa called Paramātman who is higher than the highest, who lies in the city (puriśayam) — that is, who has entered into all bodies. On this very meaning, two illuminating verses (mantras) follow.
PR_C05_V06: The three mātrās are death-bearing when used [separately]; but when joined to one another, not divorced, and properly applied to the actions outer, inner, and middle — the knower trembles not. (6)
PR_C05_V06::block-0:
“The three” — three in number — namely a-kāra, u-kāra, and ma-kāra, are the mātrās of the Oṅkāra. They are mṛtyumatyaḥ — “endowed with death,” that is, those for which death exists. By etymology, mṛtyur yāsāṃ vidyate tā mṛtyumatyaḥ — “those of which death is the property,” meaning those that have not transcended the sphere of death; in fact, they remain within the sphere of death. These mātrās, when used in the actions of meditation upon the Self [singly], lead only to mortal results.

Further, anyonyasaktāḥ — “mutually attached,” connected with one another. Anaviprayuktāḥ — to dissect: viprayuktāḥ are those that are applied separately, each to its own single object exclusively; not so applied are aviprayuktāḥ; not aviprayuktāḥ are an‑aviprayuktāḥ. The double negation establishes: at one and the same time of meditation, conjointly, they are applied. To the three actions — bāhya, ābhyantara, madhyama — meaning the yogic actions of meditation upon the Puruṣas situated respectively in the waking, dream, and deep-sleep states — when these mātrās are properly used, perfectly applied at the time of true meditation, the knower (jñaḥ) — that is, the yogin who knows the aforesaid division of the Oṅkāra — trembles not, does not falter.

For such a knower no trembling can arise. Why? Because the Puruṣas of waking, dream, and deep sleep, together with their respective stations, are seen as having the form of the three mātrās, that is, as having the form of the Oṅkāra-Self itself. He who thus knows has become the Self of all and is of the very nature of Oṅkāra — wherefrom would he tremble, or in what?
PR_C05_V07: By the Ṛks [one wins] this [world]; by the Yajus, the inter-space; by the Sāmans, that which the wise teach. By the Oṅkāra alone, as the abode, the knower attains all that — and that which is the peaceful, the unaging, the immortal, the fearless, the supreme. (7)
PR_C05_V07::block-0:
The second mantra serves to gather together the entire meaning. By the Ṛks one attains “this world” — the world characterised by men. By the Yajus, the inter-space presided over by Soma. By the Sāmans, that which is third — the world of Brahman. The kavayaḥ — the wise, the learned, those endowed with knowledge alone, not the ignorant — declare these. The threefold world of this kind the knower follows after — anveti — by means of the Oṅkāra as instrument, of the form of the lower Brahman.

By that very Oṅkāra, that which is the supreme imperishable Brahman, called Satya and Puruṣa — śāntam, peaceful, that is, free of all distinctions of waking, dream, deep sleep, and the like, devoid of all proliferation of phenomena — and therefore ajaram, free of decay; amṛtam, free of death; therefore, since free of all transformations such as decay, abhayam, fearless; and just because fearless, param, supreme, unsurpassed.

That too he follows after by means of the Oṅkāra alone as the āyatana, that is, as the means of going. The word iti is for the conclusion of the sentence. Thus the Oṅkāra is at once the lower means yielding the threefold world and the higher means yielding the unsurpassed Brahman — pravṛtti and nivṛtti rest alike upon it, distinguished only by the upāsaka's grasp.
PR_C06_V01: Then Sukeśas Bhāradvāja questioned him: Sir, Hiraṇyanābha, the prince of Kosala, having approached me, asked this question: ‘Bhāradvāja, do you know the sixteen-fold Puruṣa?’ I said to that prince: ‘I do not know him; if I had known him, why should I not have told you? He who speaks an untruth verily withers, root and all; therefore I dare not speak untruth.’ He silently mounted his chariot and went forth. I ask of you: where is that Puruṣa? (1)
PR_C06_V01::block-0:
“Then Sukeśas Bhāradvāja questioned him.” It has already been declared that the entire universe — characterised by effect and cause — together with the vijñānātman, comes to perfect rest in the supreme Imperishable at the time of deep sleep.
