By implication, it is established that at the time of cosmic dissolution too, the universe rests in that very Imperishable, and from that very Imperishable it is born; for there is no propriety in an effect coming to rest in what is not its cause. And it has been said: ‘from the Self this prāṇa is born’ (Pr. Up. 3.3).

The settled doctrine of all the Upaniṣads is that the supreme good arises from the perfect knowledge of that which is the root of the world. Just before, it was also said: ‘He becomes omniscient, he becomes all’ (Pr. Up. 4.10). Therefore, where is that Imperishable, called Satya and Puruṣa, that is to be known? — this question is raised in order to answer that. The narration of the previous incident also serves to indicate the rarity of this knowledge, so that seekers of liberation may apply themselves with special effort towards its attainment.

“Sir, Hiraṇyanābha by name, born in Kosala — hence Kausalya — a prince by birth a Kṣatriya, having approached me, asked this very question. ‘Sixteen-fold’ — that Puruṣa in whom sixteen members called kalās are superimposed by avidyā as if they were limbs of the Self — that Puruṣa is the ‘sixteen-fold’ one. Bhāradvāja, do you know that sixteen-fold Puruṣa?’ To that prince, the youth thus questioning, I said: ‘I do not know this one whom you ask about.’

Even when I had spoken thus, he could not entertain the thought that I was ignorant. Hence I gave a reason for my ignorance: ‘If somehow I did know this Puruṣa about whom you ask, why would I not tell you, who are an excellent disciple and a true seeker — that is, why would I not speak it forth?’

Further, observing that he still did not believe, I added, in order to convince him: ‘Verily, root and all, that one withers — he who, making the Self otherwise than what it is, speaks an untruth, that is, an unreal meaning — he dries up, perishes, severed from this world and the next.’ Since I know it to be so, I dare not speak untruth like a fool.

That prince, thus convinced, ashamedly mounted his chariot in silence and departed as he had come. Thus it is established here that knowledge must be imparted by him who knows to one who has approached duly and is fit; and that untruth must not be spoken under any condition whatsoever. ‘That very Puruṣa I ask of you (tvā), as one who lies like a thorn lodged in my heart, awaiting to be known: where does that Puruṣa, who is to be known, abide?’
PR_C06_V02: To him he said: Here itself, within the body, dear one, is that Puruṣa, in whom these sixteen kalās arise. (2)
PR_C06_V02::block-0:
“To him he said.” Here itself, within the body — in the space within the lotus of the heart — O dear one (saumya), is that Puruṣa; he is not to be sought in any other place. ‘In whom these — about to be enumerated — sixteen kalās, namely prāṇa and the rest, arise, are born.’ The Puruṣa, though truly partless, is, by avidyā, indicated as if endowed with parts through the sixteen kalās that serve as upādhis. By the removal of the superimposition of these upādhi-kalās, by means of vidyā, that Puruṣa, alone in his own kaivalya, must be shown forth. It is for this reason that the kalās — prāṇa and the rest — are described as ‘arising in him.’

For in the absolutely featureless, non-dual, pure Reality, no transaction of teaching and being taught is possible without superimposition; therefore the arising, abiding, and dissolution of the kalās are superimposed, all of which belong to the sphere of avidyā. The kalās are seen at all times only as inseparable from caitanya, the consciousness — they are seen arising, abiding, and dissolving with caitanya as their substrate.

For this very reason, certain bewildered ones think: ‘Just as ghee takes shape from contact with fire [as if it were of various forms], so caitanya itself arises and perishes moment by moment in the form of pot and the like.’ Others say: ‘On the cessation of that, all is mere void.’ Yet others, ‘The caitanya having pot and the like as its objects, is born and perishes for the eternal Self who is the cognizer.’ The Lokāyatikas hold that caitanya is a property of the elements (bhūta-dharma).

[Refutation:] But caitanya, having no decline or arising as its property, is the very Self, which appears, through the properties of the upādhis of name-and-form and the rest, [as if multiple]. This is borne out by the śrutis: ‘Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite’ (Tai. Up. 2.1.1), ‘Prajñāna is Brahman’ (Ai. Up. 3.1.3), ‘Vijñāna and bliss is Brahman’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.9.28), ‘a homogeneous mass of vijñāna’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.4.12), and the like. While the objects deviate from their own nature, caitanya never deviates; for as each thing is known, in just that way the non-deviation of caitanya is established by the very fact of being-known. ‘There is something real, but it is not known’ — this is impossible; just as one cannot say, ‘There is form being seen, but there is no eye.’ The known deviates; the knowing never deviates from its known — for in the absence of one known, there is the presence of another, and so the knowing remains. For when there is no knowing, there is no ‘known’ for anyone.

[Pūrvapakṣa, Vaināśika/Buddhist:] ‘In deep sleep, [the known] is not seen — and since the knowing too is absent in deep sleep, knowing is just as deviating in its own nature as the known.’

[Reply:] Not so. Knowing, the illuminator of the known, like a lamp, exists for the manifestation of the known; therefore, just as in the absence of what it should manifest, the absence of the lamp [of itself] is not established, so too, in deep sleep, when objects are not cognized, the absence of vijñāna is not established. For one who is not a Vaināśika cannot, in the dark when the eye does not perceive forms, infer the absence of the eye.

[Pūrvapakṣa:] ‘But the Vaināśika does posit absence of knowing in the absence of the known.’

[Reply:] Then by what is the absence of that [knowing] cognized? — let the Vaināśika tell us. Since that absence too is itself a known, it is not established in the absence of the knowing.

[Pūrvapakṣa:] ‘Knowing is non-different from the known; in the absence of the known, the absence of the knowing.’

[Reply:] No. Even absence is admitted by you to be a known. The Vaināśikas themselves admit absence as a known, and as eternal. If the knowing be non-different from that, then the knowing too becomes eternal — established. And the absence, being of the nature of knowing, has the name ‘absence’ only in word; in the highest sense, neither is the knowing absent nor non-eternal. Nor is anything cut away from us by the mere superimposition of the name ‘absence’ upon the eternal knowing.

[Pūrvapakṣa:] ‘But absence, though a known, is distinct from knowing.’

[Reply:] Then the absence of the known is not the absence of the knowing. The known is distinct from the knowing; the knowing is not [absent because of that]. Thus the doctrine that caitanya is the very imperishable Self stands firm against the Sāṅkhya, the Vaināśika, the Naiyāyika, and the Lokāyatika alike, and the kalās remain merely superimposed objects of avidyā.
PR_C06_V03: He reflected: ‘In whose departure shall I depart? In whose abiding shall I abide?’ (3)
PR_C06_V03::block-0:
It was said earlier, ‘in whom these sixteen kalās arise.’ The mention of the arising of the kalās was for the qualification of the Puruṣa; that very arising has another purpose too declared in śruti — namely, by what sequence does it occur? — and this is now expounded. The purport is also that creation is preceded by [the Puruṣa's] consciousness.

That sixteen-fold Puruṣa about whom Bhāradvāja was asked — saḥ īkṣāṃ cakre, he made an īkṣaṇa, a vision, that is, performed it — concerning the sequence and fruit of creation. How? It is told: ‘In what particular agent — when departed from the body — shall I depart? In what abiding — abode — shall I abide, that is, become abiding?’

[Pūrvapakṣa, Sāṅkhya:] But the Self is a non-doer; pradhāna alone is the doer. Therefore, having undertaken the human aim as the purpose, pradhāna proceeds in the form of mahat and the rest. Hence the assertion of agency on the part of the Puruṣa, with deliberation, is not proper — for once it is established by valid means that the agent of creation is pradhāna, with sattva and the other guṇas in equilibrium, or that they are atoms following the Lord's will, then there is no instrument for the Self's agency, given his non-duality, and there is no propriety either in the Self being agent of injurious activity for himself. For one who is conscious and acts deliberately would not bring harm upon himself. Therefore the upacāra ‘he made an īkṣaṇa’ etc. is figurative, applied to the unconscious pradhāna proceeding as if with intelligence according to a fixed sequence for the Puruṣa's purpose — like the saying ‘the king [conquers]’ is applied to a servant who accomplishes all the king's purposes.

[Reply, Siddhāntin:] Not so. Just as the Self is enjoyer, so too his agency is established. Just as the Sāṅkhya holds the Self, though pure consciousness and unchanging, to be enjoyer, so for the upholders of the Vedas, the agency of the Self in creation, preceded by īkṣaṇa, is established by the authority of śruti.

[Sāṅkhya:] ‘In our system, transformation into another category yields the Self's faults of non-eternality, impurity, and multiplicity; but if the Puruṣa be only a modification of pure consciousness, while remaining intrinsically of pure consciousness, the modification is no fault — yet for you Vedavādins, in the agency for creation, there is the very transformation into another category; hence all the faults of non-eternality, etc., would follow upon the Self.’

[Reply:] Not so. Even of one Self, the distinctions due to upādhis of name-and-form, which are the realm of avidyā, and those without upādhi, are admitted. The distinction due to upādhi, made by name-and-form rooted in avidyā, is admitted in respect of the Self for the purposes of the śāstric transactions of bondage, liberation, and the rest.

In truth, that which is without upādhi — that Reality is one, without a second, the goal to be attained, beyond the comprehension of every logician — is to be sought as the unborn, the fearless, the auspicious. There, neither agency nor enjoyership, neither action, instrument, nor fruit exists, all things being non-dual.

The Sāṅkhyas, on the other hand, having imagined agency in the Puruṣa as merely superimposed by avidyā — together with action, instrument, and fruit — and then, frightened of being scriptureless, demand the Puruṣa's enjoyership in the highest sense. Imagining pradhāna as another principle, external to the Puruṣa, real in the highest sense, they fall into the field of the intellects fashioned by other logicians and are routed.

Likewise the other logicians are routed by the Sāṅkhyas. Thus, by mutual fabrication of contradictory positions — like creatures fighting over a piece of meat, perceiving each other's claims as contradictory — they are dragged far from the highest truth. Therefore, disregarding their views, may seekers of liberation cherish the Vedānta-truth which is the vision of oneness. We mention these doctrinal faults of the logicians only by the way; not, like logicians, with full intent.

Thus it has been said in this very text: ‘while [these schools] dispute among themselves...’ — implying that only the Vedānta vision stands firm.
PR_C06_V04: He created prāṇa; from prāṇa, śraddhā, ākāśa, vāyu, jyoti, āpas, pṛthivī, indriya, manas; food; from food, vigour, austerity, mantras, action, worlds; and in the worlds, name. (4)
PR_C06_V04::block-0:
By the Lord himself the prāṇa, the chief of all, is created from the Puruṣa. How? That Puruṣa, having seen as said before, created sarva-prāṇa — that is, that which is the support of the karaṇas of all beings, the antarātman called Hiraṇyagarbha; that he created. From that prāṇa, śraddhā — the cause of all beings' engagement in auspicious karman; thence the great elements that are the substrate-causes of the means of enjoyment of the fruit of karman were created — kham (ākāśa), having sound as its quality; vāyu, qualified by its own quality of touch and by sound, and so two-quality; likewise jyoti, qualified by its own form and by the previous two qualities, sound and touch — three-quality; likewise āpas, by their own non-common quality of taste and the entry of the previous qualities — four-quality; likewise pṛthivī, by smell and the entry of the previous qualities — five-quality.

Likewise indriya, begun by those very elements, of two kinds — for the sake of cognition and for the sake of action, ten in number — and the ruler within them, of the form of doubt-and-determination, namely manas. Having thus created the body and the karaṇas of beings, for their sustenance: anna, of the form of rice, barley, and the rest. From that anna, when eaten, vīrya — power, strength, the means for engaging in all karmans. For those endowed with vīrya, tapas — the means for purification when impurity has accrued. The mantras — the Ṛk, Yajus, Sāman, Atharvāṅgirasa — which are the means for karman, accruing to those whose inner and outer instruments have been purified by tapas. Then karma, characterised by Agnihotra and the rest. Then the lokas, the fruit of karmans. And in those lokas, the names of the beings created — Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and so on.

Thus these kalās are created in dependence on the seed of avidyā and the other defects of beings — like the appearance of two moons, mosquitoes, gnats, and the like, born of an eye affected by timira, or like the diversity of objects in a dream — and they again dissolve into that very Puruṣa, leaving behind the differentiation of name and form.
PR_C06_V05: Just as these flowing rivers, having the ocean as their goal, on reaching the ocean disappear, their names and forms being dissolved, and they are simply called 'the ocean' — even so, of this Seer, these sixteen parts that have the Puruṣa as their goal, on reaching the Puruṣa disappear, and their names and forms are dissolved, and they are simply called 'the Puruṣa.' He becomes partless and immortal. Concerning this, there is this verse.
PR_C06_V05::block-0:
How? That illustration is given: just as in the world these flowing rivers — 'samudrāyaṇāḥ', meaning those whose goal, course, and very being is the ocean alone — on reaching, that is, on approaching the ocean, attain 'astam', disappearance, the effacement of name and form. And of those that have thus set, the names and forms — characterised as 'Gaṅgā', 'Yamunā' and so on — are broken up, that is, destroyed; and through that very non-difference the substance characterised as water is simply spoken of as 'the ocean.'

In just the same way as this illustration, of this Puruṣa now under discussion, of the qualities described, who is the 'paridraṣṭā' — the seer all around, the agent of seeing, that is, the very Self of seeing. Just as the sun is the agent of its own self-luminous illumination on every side, similarly these sixteen parts beginning with prāṇa that have been spoken of are 'puruṣāyaṇāḥ' — those whose 'ayana', that is, going to merge as the very Self, is the Puruṣa, just as the ocean is for the rivers. They reach the Puruṣa, attain identity-of-being with the Puruṣa, and likewise set. And of these parts the names and forms — the names beginning with 'prāṇa' and the forms appropriate to each — are broken up. And when name and form are dissolved, that reality which is not destroyed — that is the Puruṣa: thus is He spoken of by the knowers of Brahman.

He who, knowing thus, has had the path of the dissolution of the parts shown to him by the teacher — when by knowledge the parts beginning with prāṇa, which were produced by avidyā, desire and karma, have been dissolved — becomes 'akala', partless. For mortality is occasioned by the parts that are made by avidyā; on their cessation, by the very fact of partlessness, He becomes immortal. With reference to that very meaning is this verse.
PR_C06_V06: Like spokes in the hub of a chariot-wheel, in whom the parts are established — know that Puruṣa, the one to be known, so that death may not torment you.
PR_C06_V06::block-0:
'Spokes', that is, the supporting parts of a chariot-wheel that surround it; in the 'rathanābhi', the hub of the chariot-wheel, just as they are inserted and become dependent on it — even so, that is the meaning. The parts beginning with prāṇa are established in that Puruṣa during the times of origin, sustenance and dissolution; that Puruṣa, who is the very Self of the parts, who is to be known — 'puruṣa' so called either because of fullness or because of lying within the city (of the body) — know Him, that is, understand Him.

O disciples, may death not torment 'vaḥ', that is, you. If He be not known, you, having attained torment occasioned by death, would simply be sorrowful. Therefore, may that not be yours — such is the import.
PR_C06_V07: He said to them: 'This much only do I know — this supreme Brahman; there is nothing higher than this.'
PR_C06_V07::block-0: Having thus instructed those disciples, Pippalāda said to them: 'This much only is the supreme Brahman to be known — this I know, I understand. Nothing higher than this, beyond this, is there to be known' — thus he spoke, in order both to dispel any doubt in the disciples that something further yet remained unknown, and to produce in them the conviction that their goal had been attained.
PR_C06_V08: They, worshipping him, said: 'You indeed are our father, who carry us across to the other shore beyond ignorance.' Salutations to the supreme Ṛṣis! Salutations to the supreme Ṛṣis!
PR_C06_V08::block-0:
Then those disciples, having been instructed by the teacher, having become fulfilled, and seeing no other recompense for the knowledge — what did they do? It is told: worshipping, that is, paying homage at his feet by scattering handfuls of flowers and by prostration with the head. What did they say? It is said: 'You indeed are our father — for of this Brahman-body, eternal, free from old age and death, fearless, you are the begetter through knowledge.

It is you alone who carry us across to the supreme shore — the shore characterised by non-return, called liberation — as if across a great ocean, from the great ocean of ignorance, which is impassable on account of the crocodiles in the form of birth, old age, death, disease and sorrow arising from perverted knowledge, that is, from avidyā, by means of the boat of knowledge. Therefore fatherhood toward us is more fitting in your case than in any other's. The other father too begets only the body, yet he is held most worthy of reverence in the world; what then need be said of one who confers absolute fearlessness?' — such is the import.

'Salutations to the supreme Ṛṣis' — to those who have transmitted the lineage of the knowledge of Brahman. The repetition 'Salutations to the supreme Ṛṣis' is for the sake of reverence.
